reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Aggressive malignancy arising from the mesothelial lining of the pleura, strongly linked to prior asbestos exposure with a latency often of several decades
Typically presents with progressive breathlessness, a unilateral pleural effusion, and non-pleuritic chest wall pain
Imaging shows a nodular or rind-like pleural thickening that encases the lung, frequently with a contracted hemithorax
Diagnosis requires tissue, ideally by image-guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy, since cytology alone is often insufficient
Epithelioid, sarcomatoid, and biphasic subtypes differ in behaviour, with sarcomatoid carrying the worst outlook
Unlike benign pleural plaques it is diffuse, invasive, and carries a poor prognosis
Management is usually multimodality, combining systemic therapy with selected surgery and radiotherapy, alongside effusion control and palliative care
Recognised as an industrial disease in many jurisdictions, so exposure documentation and compensation advice are important
reference.pathophysiology: Asbestos fibres retained in the pleura, particularly amphibole types, cause chronic inflammation, oxidative injury, and genetic damage to mesothelial cells over many years. Loss of tumour-suppressor function and accumulated somatic mutations drive malignant transformation of the mesothelium. The tumour then spreads diffusely along the pleural surfaces, forming a thickened rind that encases the lung, invades the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinal structures, and commonly produces a recurrent exudative and often bloody effusion. Progressive encasement restricts lung expansion and causes the characteristic contracted hemithorax.
additionalDifferentials: Benign asbestos-related pleural plaques and diffuse pleural thickening
Solitary fibrous tumour of the pleura
Tuberculous or other chronic infective pleuritis
Thymic or other mediastinal tumour extending to the pleura
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax to characterise pleural thickening and assess extent
Thoracoscopic or image-guided pleural biopsy with immunohistochemistry for definitive diagnosis
Pleural fluid analysis, recognising that cytology alone is often inconclusive
PET-CT to assess disease extent and guide staging
MRI where chest wall or diaphragmatic invasion needs clarification
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness with a large or rapidly reaccumulating unilateral effusion
Persistent chest wall pain, especially if boring or radiating along an intercostal distribution
A shrinking hemithorax with nodular circumferential pleural thickening
Weight loss, sweats, and constitutional decline
New palpable chest wall mass or biopsy-tract seeding
reference.prognosis: Overall prognosis is poor, with survival usually measured in months to a small number of years; the epithelioid subtype and earlier-stage, resectable disease fare relatively better, whereas sarcomatoid tumours carry the worst outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming benign pleural plaques exclude mesothelioma in a patient with asbestos exposure
Relying on pleural fluid cytology alone and missing the diagnosis
Delaying tissue diagnosis and specialist referral in a patient with an unexplained persistent effusion
Overlooking the potential for tumour seeding along biopsy or drain tracts
Failing to document occupational exposure for medico-legal and compensation purposes
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: First-line systemic therapy with platinum plus pemetrexed chemotherapy, or combination immunotherapy with nivolumab and ipilimumab, particularly for non-epithelioid disease
Radical surgery such as pleurectomy-decortication within a multimodality approach for selected fit patients with early epithelioid tumours
Radiotherapy for palliation of chest wall pain or as part of multimodality treatment
Control of recurrent pleural effusion by talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter
Attention to symptom control, particularly pain and breathlessness, with early palliative care input
Document asbestos exposure and advise on compensation, industrial injury benefit and statutory reporting
Manage through a specialist mesothelioma multidisciplinary team and consider enrolment in clinical trials
